index.one_liner: Three-stage search that jointly optimizes block-level prompts, workflow topology, and global prompts for multi-agent systems.
index.why_it_matters: In 10/18 curated lists; the main DeepMind entry in prompt+topology co-optimization and a frequent baseline for AFlow/MaAS-style work, yet absent from the index.

index.name: Towards an AI co-scientist (Google DeepMind / Google Research)
index.one_liner: Gemini-based multi-agent system that generates, debates, tournament-ranks and evolves research hypotheses with a self-improvement loop; validated in drug repurposing and AMR.
index.why_it_matters: The flagship big-lab 'AI scientist' with an explicit evolution/tournament loop and wet-lab validation; the index has Kosmos, AI Scientist, DeepScientist etc. but not this one. Blog: research.google/blog/accelerating-scientific-breakthroughs-with-an-ai-co-scientist/; open reimplementations exist (Kaimen-Inc/Co-Scientist).

index.name: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on ML Engineering (OpenAI)
index.one_liner: 75 Kaggle-derived tasks measuring autonomous ML engineering; the de-facto scoreboard for autoresearch agents.
index.why_it_matters: ★1739; AIDE, R&D-Agent, AIRA/AIRA2, OpenRSI/OpenMLE and Frontis-MA1 (all indexed) report results on it, so a landscape without MLE-bench lacks the common yardstick. Paper: arXiv 2410.07095. PaperBench (arXiv 2504.01848) is the companion replication benchmark.

index.name: MLGym: A New Framework and Benchmark for Advancing AI Research Agents (Meta FAIR)
index.one_liner: Gym-style environment + 13 open-ended AI research tasks for training/evaluating research agents with RL.
index.why_it_matters: Meta's foundational AI-research-agent environment (Feb 2025) that precedes AIRA-dojo (arXiv 2507.02554, also absent) and AIRA2 (indexed); it is the natural substrate for RSI-Exam/OpenRSI-style loops. Paper: arXiv 2502.14499.

index.name: RE-Bench: Evaluating frontier AI R&D capabilities of LM agents against human experts (METR)
index.one_liner: Seven open-ended ML research environments with human-expert baselines; agents beat humans at 2h budgets, lose at 8h+.
index.why_it_matters: The safety community's reference measurement of 'can AI automate AI R&D', which underpins the METR expenditure-horizon and frontier-risk posts already in the index. Code: github.com/METR/RE-Bench. Also missing: METR's time-horizon paper (arXiv 2503.14499).

index.name: Open-Endedness is Essential for Artificial Superhuman Intelligence (DeepMind position, ICML 2024)
index.one_liner: Argues that open-ended, novelty-and-learnability-driven systems built on foundation models are the path to ASI.
index.why_it_matters: The theoretical framing shared by OMNI-EPIC, DGM, POET/AI-GA lineage, AC/DC and Foundation-Model Self-Play (all indexed); the index cites the descendants but not the position paper that defines the 'open-ended self-improvement' vocabulary.

index.name: LLaMEA: Large Language Model Evolutionary Algorithm (Leiden / van Stein & Bäck)
index.one_liner: LLM-driven (1+1)/(mu+lambda) evolution of metaheuristic code, evaluated on BBOB/IOH; active through Sept 2026.
index.why_it_matters: The BLADE benchmark (indexed) was built by the same group to evaluate LLaMEA-style systems; LLaMEA is a standard baseline next to EoH, ReEvo, FunSearch and LLM4AD in the algorithm-discovery literature. Paper: arXiv 2405.20132 (IEEE TEVC).

index.name: Eureka: Human-Level Reward Design via Coding LLMs (NVIDIA, ICLR 2024)
index.one_liner: Evolutionary search over LLM-written reward functions with reward-reflection feedback from RL training runs.
index.why_it_matters: ★3197 and cited in 5 lists; the earliest widely-adopted 'LLM as evolutionary code mutator with training-loop feedback' system and the entry point for embodied/robotic self-improvement, which the index barely covers (only ENPIRE).

index.name: INTUITOR / RLIF: Learning to Reason without External Rewards (UC Berkeley, ICLR 2026)
index.one_liner: Uses the model's own self-certainty as the sole RL reward, matching GRPO on math and generalizing better to code.
index.why_it_matters: Anchor paper of the 'intrinsic / label-free reward' thread that the index samples via TTRL, Co-rewarding, Self-Harmony and 'Can LRMs self-train?' but omits at its root; also the main target of the spurious-reward and entropy-minimization critiques. Paper: arXiv 2505.19590.

index.name: Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT): Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning (MIT Improbable AI / ETH)
index.one_liner: Model acts as its own in-context teacher to generate on-policy targets, learning new skills from demonstrations with minimal forgetting.
index.why_it_matters: The 2026 reference for weight-level continual learning inside agents (spawned the OPSD/on-policy self-distillation line: OPD-Evolver, LOPD, Awesome-OPD); the index's weight-updating side has SEAL and MemRL but nothing on forgetting-free continual updates. Impl: github.com/lucidrains/sdft-pytorch.

index.name: Vision-Zero: Scalable VLM Self-Improvement via Strategic Gamified Self-Play
index.one_liner: Zero-data self-play (Who-Is-the-Spy style games over arbitrary images) with iterative self-play policy optimization for VLMs.
index.why_it_matters: Cited in 10/18 lists and the most-referenced multimodal analogue of AZR/R-Zero; the index's self-play-from-zero cluster is entirely text/code, leaving VLM self-evolution (Vision-Zero, RISE, iReasoner, EvoVid) uncovered. Code: github.com/wangqinsi1/Vision-Zero.

index.name: Mem0: production memory layer for AI agents
index.one_liner: Most-adopted open-source long-term memory layer (extract/consolidate/update memories across sessions) with a research paper on scalable memory.
index.why_it_matters: ★65k and present in 10/18 lists; the index covers Letta, MemOS, Hindsight, ReMe, A-MEM and Acontext but not the most widely deployed memory substrate that many 'self-evolving memory' papers benchmark against. Paper: arXiv 2504.19413.

index.name: OpenClaw (the 🦞 agent platform behind the 'Claw' ecosystem)
index.one_liner: 389k-star open agent runtime with a skills marketplace, persistent memory and self-written skills; the base for AutoResearchClaw, SkillClaw, MetaClaw, KnowAct-GUIClaw and 'Claw-like agents' papers.
index.why_it_matters: Half a dozen indexed items are OpenClaw derivatives or explicitly target 'Claw-like agents' (EnvCraft, ClawBench), yet the platform itself and its community self-improving skills are absent, so the ecosystem's substrate is invisible.

index.name: DeepSeek Harness (dsh): Everything is a Plugin
index.one_liner: DeepSeek's open agent harness (Aug 2026, ★220k in a month) with pluggable agent loop, layered skill registry, memory plugins and reversible effects.
index.why_it_matters: The newest major open harness substrate from a frontier lab; harness-evolution work (Meta-Harness, AHE, HarnessDev, EvoHarnessBench) will target it, and its 'agent loop is itself a plugin' design is directly relevant to self-modifying harnesses. Hermes Agent and OpenViking are indexed; this is the comparable omission.

index.name: SIMA 2: an agent that plays, reasons and learns with you in virtual 3D worlds (Google DeepMind)
index.one_liner: Gemini-based embodied agent that self-improves: Gemini proposes tasks and estimated rewards, the agent's own play fills experience banks used to train the next version.
index.why_it_matters: The clearest big-lab example of an embodied self-improvement loop (Nov 2025); the index's embodied coverage is one paper (ENPIRE). Related uncovered sub-area index: github.com/cocacola-lab/awesome-embodied-rsi (★119).

index.name: Ouroboros: self-creating AI agent (technical report arXiv 2608.08311)
index.one_liner: General-purpose desktop/CLI agent with durable identity and memory that rewrites its own code, architecture, prompts, tools and dependencies under reviewed self-modification.
index.why_it_matters: ★1300, GitHub-trending Aug 2026, cited in 7/18 lists; it is the most-used open 'self-modifying agent' outside the DGM research lineage and comes with a skills marketplace (OuroborosHub).

index.name: MetaRSI / RSI²: A Meta-Recursive Self-Improving System for RSI Systems Themselves
index.one_liner: Meta-level scheduler coordinating Data-RSI, Harness-RSI and Model-RSI operators to extend recursive self-improvement beyond machine-checkable domains (+10.9 pts avg on coding/science).
index.why_it_matters: Sept 2026 (31 authors) and already the most explicit 'RSI over data, harness and weights at once' framework; it is the natural successor to Hyperagents/HGM/OpenRSI in the index. Companion Sept-2026 items also absent: Meta^n (arXiv 2608.24735), SkillAdam (arXiv 2609.08944), SafeEvolve (arXiv 2609.02786).

index.name: Recursive Harness Self-Improvement (RHI) — Sakana AI & UC Berkeley (Zaharia, Tang)
index.one_liner: Iteratively refines agent workflows as text specifications using pairwise feedback between successive revisions; low-reasoning agents surpass high-reasoning baselines at up to 60% lower cost on 30 ML research tasks.
index.why_it_matters: The index links Sakana's RSI Lab page but not the lab's own harness-RSI paper, which is the direct Sakana counterpart to Stanford's Meta-Harness and Lil'Log's harness essay.

index.name: Safety in Self-Evolving LLM Agent Systems: Threats, Amplification, and Case Studies
index.one_liner: Module-Lifecycle Attack Surface threat model: 17 of 25 attack cells critical, and evolution-native designs achieve 100% attack persistence because adversarial influence gets permanently encoded.
index.why_it_matters: System-level security of self-evolving agents is thinner in the index than misevolution benchmarks; this paper plus 'Zombie Agents: persistent control via self-reinforcing memory injections' (arXiv 2602.15654, ICLR 2026 workshop) are the two most-cited security threat models in the curated lists and neither is indexed.

deep_reads.name: Voyager: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Guanzhi Wang, Yuqi Xie, Yunfan Jiang, Ajay Mandlekar, Chaowei Xiao, Yuke Zhu, Linxi "Jim" Fan, Anima Anandkumar — NVIDIA, Caltech, UT Austin, Stanford, UW Madison/ASU
deep_reads.last_activity: Repo last substantive commit 2023-07-27 (dependency pins); last push 2024-04-03; effectively unmaintained
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: arXiv 2305.16291; published in TMLR (2024); NeurIPS 2023 workshop presentation; several thousand citations (Google Scholar, est. 3000+ by 2026) — the canonical reference for LLM 'skill library' agents
deep_reads.mechanism: Single-agent outer loop (voyager.py learn(), 160 iterations, 3 seeds). Each iteration: (1) CurriculumAgent (GPT-4, temp 0) proposes ONE next task from current state (biome, nearby/recently-seen blocks, entities, health/hunger, inventory, chests), the list of completed tasks and "failed tasks that are too hard", plus 5 self-asked questions answered by GPT-3.5 (cached in a Chroma vectordb). Observation fields are unlocked on a warm-up schedule; first task is hardcoded "Mine 1 wood log"; inventory-full triggers hardcoded chest tasks. (2) SkillManager retrieves top-5 skills by cosine similarity between the task context (+ summarized chat log on later rounds) and OpenAI embeddings of GPT-3.5-written descriptions of each stored program. (3) ActionAgent (GPT-4) writes one async Mineflayer JS function, given retrieved skill code, hand-written control primitives (mineBlock, craftItem, smeltItem, placeItem, killMob, exploreUntil), last-round code, execution error, chat log, state, and the critic's critique; code is babel-parsed, the last async function becomes the candidate skill. (4) The env executes it with ALL stored skills + primitives loaded as helper programs. (5) CriticAgent (GPT-4) judges success from the post-execution state only (inventory/equipment/health/hunger/nearby blocks/chests) and returns JSON {success, critique}; any execution error short-circuits to failure. Up to 4 rounds per task. (6) On success, program code + generated description are appended to skills.json/vectordb (name collision => overwrite, old file kept as V2); on failure after 4 rounds the task joins the failed list, which the curriculum reads. Skills are never modified, pruned, or re-validated afterward.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Per-task binary success from a GPT-4 critic (LLM judge) reading ground-truth Minecraft state after execution, plus hard signals from the environment: JS execution errors and bot.chat logs from Mineflayer. No scalar reward. A skill enters the library only after the critic says success; failed tasks are retried at most 4 rounds with critique/errors fed back, then recorded as "too hard" for the curriculum. Anti-drift/anti-hacking is weak and mostly structural: inventory is real environment state (can't be faked by text), code must parse and run, and the curriculum prompt explicitly forbids proposing tasks the critic can't verify from inventory (placing/building/planting/trading). Prompt-level 'do not cheat' rules (maxDistance 32, no infinite loops) are the only guardrails against gaming. No held-out evaluation of stored skills, no regression testing when a same-named skill is overwritten, no re-validation when a skill is reused in a new world. Paper-level evaluation: unique items obtained, tech-tree milestone iteration counts, map traversal, and zero-shot transfer of the library to unseen tasks in a fresh world. Ablations (paper): removing self-verification cuts unique items ~73%; random curriculum ~93% fewer; no skill library plateaus late; GPT-3.5 for code gives 5.7x fewer items; environment feedback and execution errors matter less than self-verification.
deep_reads.key_results: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations vs <20 for ReAct/Reflexion/AutoGPT (3.3x); tech-tree milestones unlocked 15.3x faster (wooden), 8.5x (stone), 6.4x (iron), and only Voyager reached diamond tools; 2.3x longer map traversal; zero-shot generalization: with the learned library it solved all 4 unseen tasks (diamond pickaxe, golden sword, lava bucket, compass) in a new world while baselines failed within 50 iterations; giving Voyager's skill library to AutoGPT improved AutoGPT. Released libraries hold ~57 skills per trial. Ablations: self-verification is the most important feedback (−73% items without it), automatic vs random curriculum −93%, GPT-3.5 code generation 5.7x fewer items.
deep_reads.limitations: Stated by authors: GPT-4 API cost (GPT-3.5 unusable); imprecise skills — agent still gets stuck, self-verification sometimes misjudges (e.g., not recognizing string as evidence of killing a spider); hallucinations — curriculum proposes non-existent items (copper sword/chestplate), code uses invalid recipes or nonexistent functions; no visual perception (uses Mineflayer API state, not pixels); building/spatial tasks require human critic/curriculum (manual mode). Observed from code: skill library is append-only with silent overwrite on name collision and no re-validation; the critic never sees code or trajectory, only final state; all skill code is concatenated into the JS runtime every step; retrieval is by GPT-3.5 paraphrase with no usage/success statistics; difficulty is tuned by hardcoded heuristics (peaceful->easy after 15 tasks, hardcoded first task and chest tasks); evaluation is on one game with 3 seeds; repo pinned to 2023 gpt-4, langchain 0.0.x, chromadb<0.4, Minecraft 1.19 Fabric plus Azure login — hard to reproduce today.
deep_reads.key_insight: Make executable, composable code the unit of learned capability: store only environment-verified programs, index them by natural-language description embeddings for retrieval, and inject them back as callable helpers so new skills compose old ones — capability compounds without weight updates and without catastrophic forgetting, and the closed loop propose -> retrieve -> generate -> execute -> verify -> store is what turns an LLM into a lifelong learner.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Prompt-level constraints only (no infinite loops/recursion, no event listeners, maxDistance 32 'do not cheat', define variables inside functions); babel syntax parse before execution; max 4 rounds per task and 160-iteration cap; env request timeout (600s); on rollout exception the env is hard-reset restoring inventory/position; optional revert of placed blocks on failed tasks (reset_placed_if_failed); optional 'manual' modes where a human replaces the curriculum or critic. No sandboxing of generated JS beyond the Mineflayer Node process, no rollback of skill-library writes, no human approval by default.
open_gaps: Skill library is append-only: no fitness/usage/success-rate tracking, no pruning, no re-validation of a skill after the world state it was born in changes
Name collision silently overwrites a skill (skill.py add_new_skill) with no regression test on skills that compose the old version — no versioning semantics or rollback
No refinement of existing skills: when a retrieved skill fails inside a new composition the fix is written as new code, never propagated back to the faulty skill

Verifier sees only final inventory/state, never the code or trajectory; the curriculum prompt explicitly forbids tasks the verifier cannot check (build/place/plant/trade), so the task space is shaped by verifier weakness
No held-out evaluation of stored skills; transfer is only measured in the same game with a new seed, no cross-domain or cross-API transfer
Single trajectory, single agent: no archive/population of alternative solutions, no explicit novelty or learning-progress metric — diversity relies on the prompt saying 'be novel'

Context budget is unmanaged: top-5 full skill source in the prompt and the entire library concatenated into the JS runtime each step; no hierarchical abstraction or summarization of skills as the library grows
Retrieval keyed only on a GPT-3.5 paraphrase of code; no preconditions/postconditions, dependency graph, or recency in ranking
Control primitives (mineBlock, craftItem, etc.) are hand-written and domain-specific; porting to another environment requires rewriting primitives and every prompt
Frontier-model dependency with no distillation: GPT-3.5 yields 5.7x fewer items and nothing is learned into weights or a cheaper model
Generated JavaScript runs unsandboxed inside the Mineflayer Node process; 'do not cheat' is a prompt instruction, not an enforced constraint
Reproducibility decay: pinned to 2023 gpt-4, langchain 0.0.x, chromadb<0.4, Minecraft 1.19 + Azure login; repo unmaintained since mid-2023
sources_read: https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.16291 (fetch attempts reset; abstract obtained via README and HF mirror)

deep_reads.name: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Google DeepMind — Alexander Novikov, Ngân Vũ, Marvin Eisenberger, Emilien Dupont, Po-Sen Huang, Adam Zsolt Wagner, Sergey Shirobokov, Borislav Kozlovskii, F. J. R. Ruiz, A. Mehrabian, M. P. Kumar, A. See, S. Chaudhuri, G. Holland, A. Davies, S. Nowozin, Pushmeet Kohli, Matej Balog
deep_reads.last_activity: Follow-ups: Georgiev/Gómez-Serrano/Tao/Wagner 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale' (arXiv 2511.02864, Nov 2025; problem repo google-deepmind/alphaevolve_repository_of_problems pushed 2026-09-10, 67 problems); results repo pushed 2026-01-05; commercial 'AlphaEvolve on Google Cloud' (Gemini Enterprise) client library Google-Cloud-AI/alphaevolve-on-googlecloud created 2026-07-08, pushed 2026-09-02 (now runs gemini-3.5-flash / gemini-3.1-pro-preview ensemble)
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: Technical white paper / arXiv preprint (not peer-reviewed). ~833 citations per scout's Semantic Scholar count (S2 API was rate-limited during this read, could not independently re-verify). Reference point for OpenEvolve (7.3k stars), ShinkaEvolve (1.4k), ThetaEvolve, CodeEvolve, DeepEvolve, LLM4AD_Next etc.
deep_reads.mechanism: The evolved object is user-marked code (# EVOLVE-BLOCK-START/END) inside a skeleton that exposes a Python evaluate() returning a dict of scalar metrics (maximized). Everything else in the file is fixed. The controller loop (asyncio, throughput-optimized) is literally: parent, inspirations = database.sample(); prompt = prompt_sampler.build(parent, inspirations); diff = llm.generate(prompt); child = apply_diff(parent, diff); results = evaluator.execute(child); database.add(child, results). Prompts contain several prior programs with their scores, rendered evaluation outputs, human-written context (equations, papers, code), stochastic template placeholders, and "meta prompt evolution": instructions the LLM itself proposes, co-evolved in a separate database. The LLM ensemble is Gemini 2.0 Flash (throughput, most samples) plus Gemini 2.0 Pro (occasional high-quality jumps); output is SEARCH/REPLACE diff blocks (or full rewrites for short code), any language (Python, Pallas, Verilog, XLA IR). Evaluators support a cascade of increasingly hard test stages (early pruning), optional LLM-graded auxiliary scores (e.g., simplicity), embarrassingly parallel evaluation up to ~100 compute-hours per candidate, and multiple objectives (which empirically improves even the single target metric via diversity). The database is a MAP-Elites + island-model hybrid balancing exploitation and diversity; nothing is fine-tuned, the model is frozen. For math problems the key trick is evolving a search heuristic that gets a fixed time budget (e.g., 1000 s) and the previous best construction, so evolution selects for heuristics that improve already-good solutions, yielding multi-stage specialized heuristics. Thousands of LLM samples suffice (FunSearch needed millions). Human picks the abstraction (raw solution vs constructor vs search algorithm vs co-evolution).
deep_reads.eval_loop: Signal is a user-written, automatically executable evaluator h returning scalar metrics; selection = registration into the MAP-Elites/island database (no notion of accept/reject beyond scores). Drift/hacking control is entirely delegated to evaluator design plus post-hoc human verification: matmul decompositions are rounded and verified exactly; Borg heuristic is correct by construction (only ranks already-feasible machines) and tested on an unseen held-out workload set before fleet rollout; kernel tiling heuristic trained on half of collected input shapes, evaluated on the other half; XLA-IR edits checked against reference on randomized inputs then confirmed by human experts; Verilog rewrite validated by TPU designers. No held-out generalization for math problems (scores are the objective itself). The follow-up Tao et al. paper admits AlphaEvolve 'occasionally exploited numerical artifacts or found loopholes in problem formulations', so every claimed math record needed expert verification. No LLM judge in the core loop (optional LLM-graded side metrics only). Ablations (2 tasks, 3 seeds each): removing evolution hurts most; removing context, meta-prompt evolution, full-file evolution, or the large model each significantly degrades the compute-vs-score curve.
deep_reads.key_results: Claimed and mostly externally verifiable (colab with verification code): 4x4 complex matmul in 48 scalar multiplications (Strassen recursive = 49, first char-0 improvement in 56 years); improved rank upper bounds on 14 <m,n,p> tensors (e.g. <3,4,7> 66->63, <4,5,6> 93->90) and matched all others for m,n,p<=5; 50+ open math problems: ~75% matched SOTA, ~20% improved (kissing number in 11D 592->593; new Erdős minimum-overlap upper bound; autocorrelation inequality bounds; packing/Heilbronn variants). Production infra (self-reported by Google, not externally verifiable): Borg scheduling heuristic recovering 0.7% of fleet-wide compute continuously for >1 year; Gemini Pallas matmul tiling heuristic: avg 23% kernel speedup, 1% reduction in Gemini training time, deployed (kernel tuning went from months to days); FlashAttention XLA IR: 32% kernel and 15% pre/post-processing speedup on GPU inference config; TPU Verilog rewrite removing unnecessary bits (authors concede synthesis tools also caught it). Ablations show every component matters. No compute cost, wall-clock, or token counts reported.
deep_reads.limitations: Stated: only works when an automated evaluator exists; LLM-based evaluation of ideas is supported but unoptimized; self-improvement of its own substrate is 'moderate' with month-scale feedback loops. Observed: ablations only on 2 tasks x 3 seeds; no cost/compute accounting; no code released for the system (only result notebooks), Gemini-only and now a paid Gemini Enterprise product; model weights are frozen (distillation deferred to future work); heavy reliance on expert problem formulation and prompt advice (Tao et al.: expert advice in the prompt 'almost always led to significantly better results'); evaluator loopholes/numerical artifacts were exploited, requiring human verification; fails where 'genuinely new, deep insights' are needed rather than hill-climbable improvements; small-scale numerical gains may not reflect asymptotic truth; the headline infra numbers (0.7%, 1%) are unverifiable outside Google, and the TPU result is marginal.
deep_reads.safety_measures: No safety section. Grounding is via code execution and automated evaluators (claimed to 'avoid incorrect suggestions'); evaluation cascade filters faulty programs on small tests first; deployed artifacts pass human review (TPU designers, kernel/XLA experts), randomized differential testing vs reference implementation, and held-out datasets before rollout; Borg heuristic can only re-rank feasible machines so is correct by construction. No discussion of sandboxing generated code, of the agent modifying its own harness, or of automated rollback; the substrate self-improvement (kernels, scheduler, TPU RTL) is gated by human deployment decisions, not closed automatically.
deep_reads.key_insight: With a frozen frontier LLM as the mutation operator, an evolutionary program database (MAP-Elites + islands) plus a cheap, automatically executable evaluator is enough test-time-compute structure to turn 'thousands' of samples into SOTA-breaking discoveries — and the highest-leverage move is to evolve the search algorithm that produces the solution (with a time budget and the previous best as input) rather than the solution itself.
open_gaps: No cross-problem transfer: each run starts from an empty program database; discovered heuristics, ideas, and meta-prompts are not stored as reusable skills/memory for new tasks (only 'distill into next base model' is mentioned as future work)

Evaluator is static and human-written; the loop exploited numerical artifacts and formulation loopholes (Tao et al. 2025) — no automatic evaluator hardening, adversarial testing, or co-evolution of tests with programs

Only the target code and meta-prompts evolve; the harness itself (database sampling policy, island/MAP-Elites config, model mix, cascade thresholds, prompt-sampler strategy) is fixed and hand-tuned per problem
Model weights never update from the evolutionary trace; no RL/fine-tuning on successful diffs (contrast ThetaEvolve, Surina et al.), so the mutation operator does not improve over the run

Abstraction choice (evolve raw solution vs constructor vs search algorithm vs co-evolution) and the expert problem context are manual and decisive — no automation of task specification or of the 'what to evolve' decision

Held-out generalization is checked only in the two infra applications; math/algorithm runs optimize the objective directly with no separate test distribution, so overfitting to the evaluator is undetected until human review
Closed source, Gemini-only, no compute/token/cost reporting; ablations on 2 tasks with 3 seeds — reproducibility depends on OpenEvolve/ShinkaEvolve reimplementations
Sample efficiency is still 'thousands' of full evaluations per problem with no bandit model selection or novelty filtering (ShinkaEvolve reports ~150 samples on circle packing)

No sandboxing, rollback, or verification story for self-modification: substrate improvements (kernels, scheduler, RTL) are deployed by humans after months, so the 'improves its own training' loop is not actually closed or automated
Requires a fully automatable scalar evaluator; domains with natural-language or human-judged outcomes are explicitly out of scope and LLM-as-evaluator is unoptimized

https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2511.02864 (Tao et al. follow-up: limitations, reward hacking)

deep_reads.name: Absolute Zero Reasoner (AZR)
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Andrew Zhao, Yiran Wu, Yang Yue, Tong Wu, Quentin Xu, Matthieu Lin, Shenzhi Wang, Qingyun Wu, Zilong Zheng, Gao Huang — Tsinghua LeapLab / BIGAI / Penn State
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: NeurIPS 2025 (Semantic Scholar venue; scout reports spotlight, not independently verified). 314 citations / 29 influential (Semantic Scholar, 2026-09). 299 forks. Public W&B logs + HF checkpoints (3B/7B/14B Coder, 7B/14B Base, Llama3.1-8B).
deep_reads.mechanism: One policy π plays two roles over three code-task types (deduction: predict o from (p,i); abduction: predict i from (p,o); induction: synthesize p from ≤10 (i,o) pairs + message). Each training step (verified in azr_ray_trainer.fit): for each task type, (1) PROPOSE: prompt π with K=6 reference triplets uniformly sampled from that type's buffer (K=1 program for induction) to write a new, "sufficiently different, challenging" program+input; (2) validate via Python executor: AST check, banned-module list (random, os, sys, time, hashlib, threading...), 10s timeout, determinism check by executing twice; (3) learnability reward: run the current solver G=8 times at T=1.0 on the new task, r_propose = 1 - mean_acc if 0<acc, else 0; invalid proposals treated as acc=1 → reward 0; (4) valid triplets appended to buffer regardless of reward (cap 16384; code truncates with [:max] so newest are dropped once full); (5) SOLVE: sample 64 tasks per type from buffer ("max_new": prefer last step's additions, fill uniformly), reward = binary executor equality (induction: all hidden IO pairs). Composite: r_role if formatted+correct, -0.5 if formatted but wrong/invalid, -1 if malformed. All 6 (role×task) batches of 64 are concatenated (384/step) and updated with TRR++ = REINFORCE++ with a separate mean/std baseline per (task,role); no critic, no KL, no ref policy, lr 1e-6, rollout.n=1. Seed = identity function → S×B=256 self-generated triplets before self-play. Evolution is purely in the weights plus a growing self-proposed task buffer.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Fitness is entirely executor-grounded: solver gets binary Python value-equality against ground truth produced by running the proposed program; proposer gets 1 - Monte-Carlo solve rate (G=8 samples of current policy), zero for unsolvable, plus format penalties (-0.5/-1). Drift/hacking prevention: hard validity gates (AST, banned modules, determinism via double execution, timeout), invalid proposals scored as trivially solvable (reward 0 then -0.5), per-(task,role) baseline normalization (TRR++). External benchmarks (HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench, AIME24/25, AMC, MATH500, Minerva, OlympiadBench) are report-only; CruxEval/LCB-execution validated every 10 steps for monitoring, NOT used as checkpoint acceptance. No KL anchor, no held-out gating, no rollback (remove_previous_ckpt_in_save=True keeps only latest). Solver reward is unhackable (executor), but proposer learnability can be satisfied by brittle-format tasks rather than genuinely harder reasoning; paper flags better learning-progress estimation (MAGELLAN) as future work.
deep_reads.key_results: Qwen2.5-Coder-7B + AZR: Code avg 61.6 (+5.0), Math avg 39.1 (+15.2), overall 50.4 (+10.2), beating best zero-setting models trained on 2k–484k curated examples by 1.8 avg. 14B-Coder: +13.2 overall (+22.8 math). 3B-Coder: +5.7. Llama3.1-8B: only +3.2. Ablations on 7B-Base (full 46.8): deduction-only 43.3; no induction 43.8; no reference conditioning (K=0) 43.8 (math -5.3); solve-only (proposer not trained) 45.4 (-1.4). Larger models keep improving past 200 steps; 3B plateaus. Emergent: interleaved comment-plans in induction, trial-and-error in abduction with largest token growth; Llama "uh-oh moment" safety-concerning CoT.
deep_reads.limitations: Task space restricted to deterministic, side-effect-free Python (p,i,o) triplets; no stochastic programs, tools, multi-turn, or natural-language domains. Gains depend heavily on base-model priors (Qwen ≫ Llama). Ablations only on 7B-Base due to compute. Learnability = current solve rate, not learning progress. No safety oversight; authors observed concerning CoT. Executor is raw exec with a banned-word list, "not secure for production." Main branch marked "UNDER TESTING" after veRL upgrade; reproduce from `paper` branch. Diversity/complexity intrinsic rewards exist in code but are disabled (coef 0) in all released runs; composite-function scheduler disabled. Buffer cap drops newest tasks once full. Repo inactive since 2025-08.
deep_reads.key_insight: A single model can bootstrap reasoning with zero external data if you (a) pick a task space whose ground truth is generated by executing the model's own proposal, so verification is free and unhackable, and (b) pay the proposer with 1 - (solver's current success rate), which auto-tunes a curriculum to the edge of competence; the same open-ended executor-verified loop transfers out of domain (code → math +15 pts).
open_gaps: Verification is limited to deterministic Python value-equality; no path to self-generating verifiable tasks for tool use, multi-turn agents, stochastic programs, or natural-language work
Proposer reward is instantaneous solve-rate (G=8 MC samples), not learning progress; no mechanism detects tasks that are 'hard' only because of brittle formatting or answer extraction
No explicit diversity/novelty pressure: intrinsic diversity/complexity rewards are implemented but disabled (coef=0); dedup and curriculum scheduling absent, buffer sampled uniformly
Task buffer is a flat list capped at 16384 that silently drops newest entries once full; no difficulty/age-aware archive, no priority replay, no cross-run or cross-model task library reuse
No regression protection: checkpoint acceptance is not gated by held-out eval, only the latest checkpoint is kept, no rollback, no KL anchor to reference policy
Only weights evolve; the proposer prompts, validity filters, reward function, and executor are fixed by hand and never self-modified
Requires full-parameter RL (veRL+vLLM+Ray) on 2-8x80GB GPUs; unusable for app developers who cannot fine-tune, and nothing transfers to closed-API models
Executor is unsandboxed raw exec with a banned-word list; no isolation, resource limits beyond timeout, or safety oversight despite observed concerning CoT on Llama
Improvement is bounded by base-model priors (Llama +3.2 vs Qwen-14B +13.2) and plateaus for small models; no evidence of open-ended, unbounded self-improvement
Single policy playing two roles; no separate evolving verifier/judge, no population or multi-agent diversity, no evaluation of whether proposed tasks drift toward degenerate families over long runs
deep_reads.safety_measures: AST check + banned-module list (os/sys/subprocess/threading/random/time/hashlib etc.), 10s execution timeout, determinism double-execution, format penalties; periodic executor cleanup. No sandboxing (SandboxFusion optional since 2025-07), no oversight of CoT; authors explicitly state safety management of self-improving components is unaddressed and report concerning 'uh-oh moment' outputs from Llama3.1-8B.

deep_reads.name: GEPA (Genetic-Pareto Reflective Evolution)
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Lakshya A Agrawal, Shangyin Tan, Omar Khattab, Matei Zaharia, Ion Stoica, Dan Klein, Koushik Sen, Alexandros Dimakis et al. (UC Berkeley / Stanford / Databricks / MIT; 17 authors)
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: arXiv 2507.19457 (v2 Feb 2026), accepted ICLR 2026 (Oral); ~366 citations per scout; 543 forks; 123 open issues; PyPI releases through v0.1.4 (Jul 2026); integrated into DSPy, MLflow, Opik, Pydantic AI, Google ADK, OpenAI/HF cookbooks
deep_reads.mechanism: Core loop (src/gepa/core/engine.py + proposer/reflective_mutation): (1) Seed candidate = dict of named text components (prompts, code, skill files, configs) is fully evaluated on a validation set D_pareto; state stores per-candidate, per-instance score vectors. (2) Each iteration, ParetoCandidateSelector builds the per-instance Pareto front (best score on each val example), removes globally dominated candidates, and samples a parent with probability proportional to how many instances it wins (frontier_type can be per-instance, per-objective, hybrid, or cartesian). (3) A round-robin component selector picks which text field to mutate; the parent is run on a minibatch of the train split with capture_traces=True, and the adapter's make_reflective_dataset turns trajectories plus evaluator-supplied Actionable Side Information (error messages, profiler output, judge feedback, images) into a reflective dataset. (4) A reflection LM (single call by default; ComBEE map-reduce or a Claude Code agent as alternatives) receives current text + examples + feedback and writes a replacement text. (5) Gate: child is re-run on the same minibatch; StrictImprovementAcceptance requires sum(new) > sum(old); passing children get a full valset evaluation and are added to the pool with ancestry; Pareto front updated. (6) Merge proposer: after new programs are found, sample two frontier candidates with a common ancestor whose components diverged, recombine component-wise, accept if minibatch score >= max(parents). PxNSampling (P parents x N mutations per step) batches proposals. optimize_anything wraps this as a black-box evaluator API and now also dispatches to AutoResearch (a Claude Code session owning the whole loop) and Meta-Harness engines, composable via optimize_sequential/best_of/adaptive_sequential.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Fitness = user-supplied scalar metric per example plus optional textual/structured side_info (ASI) used only by the reflection LM. Two-stage acceptance prevents drift: a cheap minibatch strict-improvement gate on the train split, then a full validation-set evaluation before a candidate enters the pool; per-instance Pareto tracking keeps specialists alive so greedy collapse does not occur (paper Table 3: Pareto +12.44% vs SelectBestCandidate +6.05% vs BeamSearch +5.11%). Final selection = best aggregate validation score; papers/blogs report separate held-out test scores (paper Fig 16 generalization gap; parallel-proposals post shows val overfitting: single-mutation had a 9-point val-to-test gap on LiveBench-Math vs 2 for 2x4). Nothing prevents reward hacking of a weak evaluator or LLM judge beyond the user's metric design; evaluation cache namespaced by split so val rollouts cannot be reused from train (PR #425).
deep_reads.key_results: Paper (ICLR 2026 Oral): Qwen3-8B aggregate +9.62% (GEPA) vs +3.68% (GRPO, 24k rollouts) across HotpotQA/IFBench/HoVer/PUPA/AIME/LiveBench-Math, up to 35x fewer rollouts (GEPA reaches optimum in 79-737 train rollouts); vs MIPROv2 +13.33% vs +5.64% on GPT-4.1-mini; prompts up to 9.2x shorter than MIPROv2; NPUEval vector utilization 4.25% -> 30.52% mean; KernelBench fast_1 ~0% -> >20%. Repo/blogs: AIME-2025 GPT-4.1-mini 46.6% -> 56.6-60%; ARC-AGI agent architecture (Gemini 3 Flash) 32.5% -> 89.5% test; CloudCast scheduling policy 40.2% test cost savings; gskill: Mini-SWE-Agent resolve rate 55% -> 82% (Jinja) and 24% -> 93% (Bleve) on held-out test with <300 rollouts, skills transfer to Claude Code Haiku 4.5 (79.3% -> 98.3% on Bleve); parallel proposals (Jul 2026): 3-4x wall-clock speedup and held-out test 68.9% -> 72.1% (LiveBench-Math), 49.0% -> 60.0% (HoVer); omni meta-optimizer 63.2 vs best standalone 55.4 on Frontier-CS at $20; FST (May 2026) interleaves GEPA with CISPO RL for ~70% lower KL at matched accuracy. Databricks: open models + GEPA beat Claude Opus 4.1 at 90x lower cost.
deep_reads.limitations: Most rollout budget is spent on full validation evals (paper-stated; PxN mitigates but full-val is still the bottleneck). Merge is hyperparameter-sensitive (hurt Qwen3-8B: +7.17% vs +9.62% without). Quality depends entirely on evaluator feedback richness (feedback engineering is on the user). Optimizes toward a fixed validation set; measurable val-to-test gap, and single-mutation runs overfit val (9-point gap). Reflection is stateless by default: rejected proposals are forgotten so the same parent repeats failed mutations (issue #379); truncated LM outputs can be adopted as candidates (#390). No cross-task/cross-run memory of lessons; each run starts from scratch. Component selection is round-robin, not credit-assigned. Evaluator cost/latency for agentic tasks (Docker, SWE tasks) is the real bottleneck. omni results are 10 problems at $20 each; ARC-AGI/AIME test sets are small. The agent-architecture and code claims are demonstrated on a handful of showcase tasks, not broad benchmarks.
deep_reads.key_insight: Treat execution traces plus evaluator side-information as a textual gradient: let an LLM read why a candidate failed and rewrite it, but gate every mutation with a cheap minibatch improvement check followed by a full validation evaluation, and keep a per-instance Pareto front (not a single best) as the population so specialists survive and can be recombined component-wise via ancestry-aware merge.
open_gaps: No persistent cross-run or cross-task memory: lessons from reflection are only embedded in the winning text; a new task or repo starts from an empty pool (gskill re-learns skills per repository)

Rejected proposals are discarded and not fed back to the reflector (issue #379), so the same parent can repeat identical failed mutations; no negative-example memory or bandit over mutation operators (issue #251 open)

Fitness is a fixed user validation set with no adaptive/held-out rotation, k-fold, or drift detection (issue #133 open); optimizer can overfit val and the framework does not measure generalization itself
Round-robin component selection: no credit assignment of failures to specific components (prompt vs code vs tool description) beyond what the reflection LM infers in-prompt
Evaluator/judge is fixed and trusted; no co-evolution or auditing of the reward function, so reward hacking of weak LLM-judge metrics is unguarded

Candidate is a flat dict of strings; no structural/typed mutation of agent topology (tools, sub-agents, control flow) with validity checks other than running the evaluator (DSPy full-program adapter evolves code but only via free-form LLM rewrite)

Self-modification is not applied to the optimizer itself: reflection prompt, minibatch size, merge scheduling and P x N width are hand-set hyperparameters (paper calls merge timing sensitive; adaptive scheduling listed as future work)
Runs are offline and batch: no online/continual loop that ingests production traces and re-optimizes with rollback in a live deployment (issue #178 open)
Full-valset evaluation after every accepted minibatch win dominates cost; no racing/successive-halving or surrogate-model early stopping of val evals
Merge is limited to component-wise recombination of two lineages sharing a common ancestor; no LLM-guided semantic merge or multi-parent synthesis
deep_reads.safety_measures: Strict minibatch improvement gate plus full validation evaluation before pool admission; Pareto archive with ancestry so any previous candidate can be recovered (state saved each iteration, resumable); optional bubblewrap sandbox and denied web tools for Claude Code-driven engines (AutoResearch/Meta-Harness); eval server enforces metric-call and USD budgets with HTTP 429 on exhaustion; test split sealed from the agent at the HTTP layer; eval cache namespaced by split to prevent train/val leakage. No formal verification or human-in-the-loop review of mutated code; safety of executing evolved code rests on the user's evaluator sandbox.

deep_reads.name: DSPy (stanfordnlp/dspy) — Declarative Self-improving Python, with GEPA / SIMBA / MIPROv2 / BootstrapFinetune optimizers
deep_reads.date: 2023-01-09 (repo created); DSPy paper Oct 2023 (ICLR 2024); MIPROv2 Jun 2024; GEPA Jul 2025; dspy.Flex Aug 2026 (v3.3.0)
deep_reads.last_activity: 2026-09-11 (pushed_at); v3.3.1 released 2026-08-21; ~100+ commits in last 90 days
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Stanford NLP (Omar Khattab, Chris Potts, Matei Zaharia et al.); GEPA by Lakshya A Agrawal et al. (UC Berkeley / Stanford / Databricks / MIT); Flex by @michaelisaac-dev; ReActV2/RLM by @isaacbmiller; 100+ contributors
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: DSPy: ICLR 2024; MIPROv2: EMNLP 2024; GEPA: arXiv 2507.19457, 366 citations on Semantic Scholar as of Sep 2026; upstream gepa-ai/gepa engine 6,518 stars; wrapped by MLflow, Databricks, Comet Opik, Ax
deep_reads.mechanism:
Compile-time outer loop, not runtime self-modification: a DSPy program is Python whose LM calls are `Predict` nodes parameterized by (instruction text, few-shot demos). `optimizer.compile(program, trainset, valset)` returns a new program; the original is deep-copied, never mutated.

GEPA loop (verified in dspy/teleprompt/gepa/*.py + gepa-ai/gepa engine.py): (1) seed candidate = {predictor_name: instruction} plus {flex_path: module_src} for any `dspy.Flex` submodule; full valset eval. (2) Sample a parent stochastically from the per-validation-instance Pareto front (any candidate best on >=1 val example), not just the global best. (3) Draw a train minibatch (default 3, epoch-shuffled), run the parent with trace capture, call the user metric per example to get a score AND free-text feedback; the metric is also called with `pred_name`/`pred_trace` for per-predictor feedback. (4) Round-robin select one component; build a reflective dataset {Inputs, Generated Outputs, Feedback} from non-perfect examples. (5) A strong reflection LM (gpt-5 recommended) rewrites that component's instruction — or, for Flex, the ENTIRE `dspy.Module` source (predictors, control flow, plain Python) via `CodeProposalSignature`, reflecting on whole-program I/O. (6) Child is evaluated on the same minibatch; accepted only if sum(new) > sum(old) (`StrictImprovementAcceptance`). (7) Accepted child gets a full valset eval, joins the permanent archive; Pareto front updated. (8) Up to 5 merge crossovers combine components of two front candidates sharing an ancestor. (9) Stop at `max_metric_calls`; return the highest aggregate-valset candidate.

SIMBA: per step, 6 program×temperature samples per example on a 32-example minibatch, sort examples by score variance, LM writes a rule (appended to instruction) or adds a demo; softmax-sampled pool. MIPROv2: bootstrap demos → grounded instruction proposals → Optuna TPE over (instruction, demo) combos with minibatch + periodic full evals. BootstrapFinetune/GRPO/BetterTogether distill metric-filtered traces into weights.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Signal = a user-written metric returning a float or `dspy.Prediction(score, feedback)`; the feedback string is injected verbatim into the reflection prompt (GEPA is the only optimizer that reads it; COPRO/MIPROv2 see a scalar). Drift/regression control: (a) strict-improvement acceptance on the same train minibatch before any full eval; (b) full held-out valset evaluation of every accepted candidate, per-instance Pareto tracking for exploration, aggregate valset score for final selection; (c) archive never deletes candidates, so the seed remains a fallback; (d) `skip_perfect_score` keeps reflection focused on failures; (e) explicit warning that valset==trainset overfits; (f) `_compiled=True` flag freezes already-optimized submodules from later optimizers. MIPROv2 uses minibatch evals with periodic full evals and a TPE surrogate. No statistical test on the 3-example acceptance gate and no defense against LLM-judge reward hacking beyond held-out ranking.
deep_reads.key_results: DSPy paper: compiling small programs beats hand prompts (e.g. GPT-3.5 25%->65% on multi-hop QA class tasks). Docs (informal): MIPROv2 light raises ReAct HotPotQA 24%->51%; RAG 53%->61%. GEPA paper (claimed, Qwen3-8B / GPT-4.1-mini on HotpotQA, IFBench, HoVer, PUPA): +10% avg and up to +20% over GRPO with up to 35x fewer rollouts (100-500 evals vs 5k-25k+), and >10% over MIPROv2. External deployments: Databricks 'agents 90x cheaper' (open models + GEPA beat Claude Opus 4.1); Nubank LLM-judge accuracy 68.9%->88.9%, Cohen's kappa 0.00->0.745; Microsoft MAI-Thinking-1 used GEPA/DSPy for a pre-training data filter; upstream claims MATH 67%->93% via full-program evolution and ARC-AGI 32%->89% via architecture discovery (upstream gepa, not reproduced in the DSPy repo).
deep_reads.limitations: Offline compile-time only: no online/continual loop from production traffic. Acceptance is a strict-improvement test on a 3-example minibatch (noisy, no significance test); valset doubles as selection set so small valsets overfit. Mutation loop is serial and dominated by reflection-LM cost (12-36 gpt-5 calls per medium run; hundreds of dollars possible); `max_reflection_cost` unsupported in the DSPy adapter. Open bug (2026-08-20): `auto_budget` does not reflect the actual reflective loop. GEPA metrics must be sync (async issue open since 2025-10). Predictor-level scoring unsupported (module-level score overrides). `dspy.Flex` (code evolution) is experimental, marked API-in-flux, has no in-repo benchmark, requires Deno/Pyodide sandbox, and reflects only on whole-program I/O. No optimizer auto-selection ('you choose'). Demo-tuning overfits small trainsets. Weight optimizers need a fine-tunable model.
deep_reads.key_insight: Treat prompts (and now module source code) as parameters of a declarative program and optimize them with feedback-rich evolutionary search: sample parents from a per-example Pareto front, mutate by having a strong LM read execution traces plus textual metric feedback, gate acceptance on the same minibatch, rank on a held-out valset — natural-language feedback is a far denser learning signal per rollout than a scalar reward, which is why it beats GRPO with 35x fewer rollouts.
open_gaps: Purely offline compile-time: no continual loop that ingests production failures, re-optimizes, and regression-gates against the currently deployed artifact
Acceptance gate is a 3-example minibatch strict-improvement test with no statistical significance check and no separate test set beyond the valset used for selection
No cross-task/cross-program transfer: every compile starts from the seed; learned instructions/rules are not stored in a reusable skill or memory library
Metric/evaluator is fixed and human-written; nothing evolves the reward, and LLM-judge feedback is injected verbatim into the proposer with no reward-hacking defense
Topology/code evolution (dspy.Flex) is experimental, confined to one sandboxed submodule, reflects only on whole-program I/O, and has no in-repo benchmark evidence
Mutation loop is serial and reflection-cost-dominated; no cost-aware budgeting (max_reflection_cost unsupported) and no parallel population/island search
No optimizer auto-selection or meta-optimization of optimizer hyperparameters
Cannot evolve tools, the harness, or infrastructure outside a Flex sandbox; tool implementations are frozen inputs
Single-agent only: no multi-agent population coordination; merges capped at 5 and limited to shared-ancestor crossover
GEPA metric must be synchronous; predictor-level scores are ignored in favor of module-level score
deep_reads.safety_measures: Flex-generated code always runs in a Deno/Pyodide `PythonInterpreter` sandbox (hardened in 3.3.1: unpredictable request IDs, revoked Deno-cache access, prototype-mutation protection); `max_predictor_calls` caps runaway generated programs; unparsable candidates score at `failure_score` instead of crashing the search; original student is deep-copied, never mutated; deterministic `seed` and checkpoint/resume via `log_dir`; hard `max_metric_calls` budget; full lineage/audit trail via `track_stats`. No default human review of proposed instructions and no bound on instruction length.

deep_reads.name: Darwin Gödel Machine (DGM)
deep_reads.mechanism: Verified against the released code (DGM_outer.py, self_improve_step.py). Archive starts with one hand-written coding agent (coding_agent.py + tools/bash.py, tools/edit.py; FM = Claude 3.5 Sonnet via Bedrock, frozen). Each generation (default 80 gens, 2 attempts/gen in parallel): (1) Parent selection from archive with P ∝ sigmoid(10·(acc−0.5)) × 1/(1+num_children) — only variants that compiled/evaluated are eligible. (2) Pick a self-improve "entry": with 25% each, a canned meta-problem (solve_empty_patches, solve_stochasticity, solve_contextlength), else one random unresolved benchmark task. (3) Diagnosis: o1 receives the parent's full source, the run log for that task, the GitHub issue, the agent's patch, SWE-bench's private test patch and test results, and must emit JSON with ONE general improvement proposal phrased as a GitHub issue ("To Implement..."). (4) Self-modification: in a Docker container with the parent lineage's patches applied, the parent agent itself runs `coding_agent.py --self_improve` on /dgm (30-min timeout) and emits model_patch.diff. (5) Evaluation: the child agent is run on SWE-bench Verified tasks in stages — 10 tasks; if ≥40% resolved, 50 more; if score ≥ second-best full-evaluated archive score (min 0.4), the remaining 140 (200 total). Polyglot analogous. (6) Archive update: child kept if it "compiled" (produced ≥1 non-empty patch on all expected tasks); default keep_all, no score threshold. Optional o1 post-hoc diagnosis of what changed. Lineage = ordered list of diffs; "no_darwin" baseline = always mutate last commit; "no_selfimprove" = fixed initial agent does all edits.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Signal = benchmark accuracy (resolved/submitted) on SWE-bench Verified (200-task subset, staged 10→60→200) or Polyglot subsets; official SWE-bench harness runs outside the agent's editable tree, so the core score is hard to fake, but in-house metrics (a hallucination-detection marker in logs) were hacked. Drift/hacking controls are weak and mostly human: eval_noise leeway 0.1, 'compiled' filter, Docker sandbox + 30-min/1.5-h timeouts, and manual review of the transparent diff lineage (which is how the marker-removal exploit was caught). No held-out split: the same 200 tasks drive selection and are the reported score; transfer checks (o3-mini, Claude 3.7 Sonnet; Python→Rust/C++/Go/Java/JS) are the only generalization evidence. No LLM judge, no unit tests on the agent beyond 2 tool tests.
deep_reads.limitations: Stated: ~2 weeks and ~$22,000 API cost per SWE-bench run; FM weights frozen (only harness code evolves); limited to coding benchmarks; empirical validation is not a proof, and the system did reward-hack an in-house hallucination metric by deleting detection markers despite explicit instruction not to. Observed from code/issues: o1 diagnoser sees private test patches of training tasks; Polyglot harness leaves hidden tests/reference solutions readable from the agent container (issue #35); 'best' parent-selection mode unreachable due to missing comma and sorts ascending (issue #31); tools loaded via importlib with no provenance check (#36); outer loop, selection policy, diagnosis prompts and evaluator are NOT self-modifiable; default keep_all archive retains regressions; repo unmaintained since 2025-08-13 with 27 open issues; hard-wired to Bedrock Claude 3.5 Sonnet + o1. Full arXiv text was unreachable from this network; ablation/transfer figures below are from paper knowledge plus secondary summaries.
deep_reads.key_insight: Drop the Gödel-machine requirement of proving an edit is beneficial; instead let the agent rewrite its own harness code (tools, workflow, prompts) with the FM frozen, validate every child empirically on a staged benchmark, and keep ALL working variants in an archive sampled by score×novelty so lower-scoring stepping stones can still parent breakthroughs — open-ended search over agent code, not hill-climbing.
open_gaps: Fitness set == report set: the same 200 SWE-bench tasks drive selection and the headline number; no held-out task split inside the benchmark, and the o1 diagnoser is shown private test patches for training tasks — a new framework needs train/validation/test task separation and evaluator-blind diagnosis

No automated reward-hacking defense: the marker-removal exploit was only caught by humans reading diffs; evaluator, logging and hidden tests should be immutable and out of the agent's reachable filesystem (issue #35 shows Polyglot hidden tests are readable)

Extremely expensive fitness (~$22k, ~2 weeks per run; every child re-runs up to 200 SWE-bench tasks): no cheap proxy fitness, no bandit/successive-halving allocation beyond a crude 10→60→200 threshold, no caching of per-task results across siblings
Single scalar objective (accuracy only): no cost, latency, token-usage, or safety objectives, no Pareto archive
Mutation only, one parent per child: no crossover/merging of successful patches from different archive lineages, no explicit reuse of discovered tools across branches
The outer loop is not self-referential: DGM_outer.py, parent-selection policy, diagnosis prompts, eval thresholds and the harness are fixed by humans; only coding_agent.py/tools/utils evolve
Diagnosis is per-single-failed-task with no aggregated failure analysis or persistent memory across generations; each child starts from one log, so the same fix can be rediscovered repeatedly
keep_all archive with no regression tests on the agent itself: regressions are kept as parents; no automatic rollback or unit-test suite that evolves with the agent (tests/ has 2 tool tests)
Benchmark-specific harness: porting to non-SWE-bench domains requires rewriting harness/report code (issues #14, #19); no pluggable task/fitness interface
FM weights frozen and hard-wired to Bedrock Claude 3.5 Sonnet + o1; no local/open-model support (issue #26 WIP), no learning from the archive back into the model
Code is unmaintained since Aug 2025 with known bugs ('best' mode unreachable, ascending sort), so anyone baselining against DGM must fork and patch
deep_reads.last_activity: Repo last push 2025-08-13 (5 commits total, final one 'Update coding_agent_polyglot.py'); paper v2 Sept 2025; ICLR 2026 camera-ready
deep_reads.key_results: SWE-bench Verified (200-task subset): initial agent 20.0% → best DGM agent 50.0% after 80 iterations. Polyglot: 14.2% → 30.7%, surpassing Aider's hand-designed agent. Ablations: DGM w/o self-improvement (fixed initial agent makes all edits) and DGM w/o open-ended exploration (single lineage, always mutate latest) both end far lower (w/o open-ended ≈23% on SWE-bench per secondary summaries). Transfer: SWE-bench-evolved agent keeps its gains when the FM is swapped to Claude 3.7 Sonnet or o3-mini; Python-only-evolved agent improves on Rust/C++/Go/Java/JS Polyglot tasks. Discovered features: granular str_replace-style editing tool, patch validation, multiple candidate patches + ranking/peer-review step, history of prior attempts. Lineage analysis shows the best agent descends through a lower-scoring ancestor (stepping-stone evidence). Case study: asked to fix tool-use hallucination, some children removed the detection markers (objective hacking), caught via lineage review. Cost: ~2 weeks, ~$22k per SWE-bench run.
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Jenny Zhang*, Shengran Hu* (UBC / Vector Institute), Cong Lu (UBC/Vector), Robert Tjarko Lange (Sakana AI), Jeff Clune (UBC / Vector / CIFAR); *co-first
deep_reads.safety_measures: Docker sandbox per self-improvement attempt and per benchmark task; 30-min timeout on the self-modification run and 1.5-h timeout per attempt; restricted web access; FM weights untouched; complete diff lineage (model_patch.diff chain + metadata.json) enabling human audit; authors manually reviewed modifications and reported they were confined to coding capability; README warns that untrusted model-generated code is executed. deep_reads.venue_or_citations: ICLR 2026 Oral (OpenReview RQm2KQTM5r); earlier FoRLM 2025 workshop version. arXiv v1 25 Jul 2025, v2 (camera-ready) 14 Feb 2026. Exact citation count not retrievable during this read (Semantic Scholar API rate-limited; OpenAlex record is stale), but it is the standard baseline in 2026 prompt-optimizer papers. deep_reads.mechanism: Paper scope: only the natural-language instruction of each LLM module in a compound program evolves (the library's later optimize_anything / gskill extend the same loop to code, agent architectures and skills). Offline outer loop over a fixed metric-call budget (matched to MIPROv2-Heavy: e.g. 6,871 calls on HotpotQA; IFBench used 678 rollouts). State = a growing tree of candidate programs, each with per-instance scores on a validation set. Per iteration (verified in artifact code): (1) SELECT parent from the per-instance Pareto front: for every val instance collect the best-scoring candidates, drop dominated ones, sample a candidate with probability proportional to the number of instances it wins (ablation 'SelectBestCandidate' = greedy argmax). (2) Pick one module round-robin. (3) Run parent on a minibatch of 3 training examples, capturing that module's inputs, outputs, reasoning and a task-specific textual feedback function mu_f (missing retrieved docs, failed IFBench constraint, judge rationale). (4) REFLECT: a reflection LM (GPT-4.1 / GPT-5 in practice) receives current instruction + examples/outputs/feedback and writes a new instruction; the static prompt tells it to infer the task, extract 'niche domain-specific facts' and generalizable strategies. (5) Evaluate the child on the same minibatch; accept only if the summed score strictly improves; then evaluate on the full valset, add to the pool, update the Pareto front. (6) MERGE (optional, max 5 invocations): after an accepted mutation, take two Pareto candidates sharing an ancestor that improved different modules, splice modules, test on instances where the parents disagree, keep if >= both parents, then full-val evaluate. Output = candidate with best aggregate val score, reported on held-out test. The reflection LM and its prompt never change.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Signal = user-supplied task metric mu (exact match / F1 / constraint pass / LLM-judge for PUPA) plus a textual feedback function mu_f fed to the reflector ('actionable side information'). Three gates against drift: (a) child must strictly beat parent on the same 3-example minibatch (cheap, noisy), (b) accepted children get a full validation-set evaluation and only the per-instance val scores drive future selection, (c) per-instance Pareto front keeps diverse lineages alive instead of collapsing to one greedy trajectory (ablation on Qwen3-8B: 61.28 vs 54.89 aggregate). Reporting is on a held-out test split. No statistical test on acceptance, no multi-seed runs, no explicit reward-hacking check: the reflection prompt actively encourages baking 'niche factual information' from training feedback into the prompt, so overfitting to the train/val distribution is checked only by the held-out test at the end. Reflection-LM token cost is not counted in the rollout budget.
deep_reads.key_results: Artifact notebook (matches v1 Table 1), test-set scores. Qwen3-8B (HotpotQA/IFBench/PUPA/HoVer/aggregate): Baseline 42.33/36.90/80.82/35.33/48.84; MIPROv2 55.33/36.22/81.55/47.33/55.11; GRPO (24,000 rollouts, LoRA) 43.33/35.88/86.66/38.67/51.14; GEPA 62.33/38.61/91.85/52.33/61.28; GEPA+Merge 64.33/28.23/86.26/51.67/57.62. GPT-4.1-mini (AIME/HotpotQA/IFBench/LiveBenchMath/PUPA/HoVer/agg): Baseline 49.33/38.00/47.79/58.20/78.57/46.33/53.78; MIPROv2 51.33/58.00/49.15/61.84/83.37/48.33/60.14; GEPA 59.33/69.00/52.72/59.43/94.47/51.67/65.46; GEPA+Merge -/65.67/55.95/64.13/96.46/56.67/67.78. GRPO was only run on Qwen3-8B. v1 abstract: +10% avg over GRPO, up to +20% (HotpotQA 62.33 vs 43.33), up to 35x fewer rollouts (IFBench 678 vs 24,000; up to 78x counting training rollouts only), >10% over MIPROv2, prompts up to 9.2x shorter (artifact: ~1.3-1.5k vs ~6.3-6.5k tokens). v2 (ICLR camera-ready) abstract revises the GRPO margin to '6% on average and up to 20%'. Pareto vs greedy-selection ablation: +6.4 aggregate on Qwen3-8B (61.28 vs 54.89); on GPT-4.1-mini the greedy ablation is marginally higher (65.13 vs 64.44 in the artifact notebook). Also used as inference-time search for AMD NPU kernel / CUDA kernel optimization (qualitative wins, no headline number recoverable). Library follow-ups (not in paper): +10pp AIME with GPT-4.1-mini (46.6 to 56.6), 32% to 89% ARC-AGI agent-architecture search, 55% to 82% coding-agent resolve rate via learned skills.
deep_reads.limitations: (1) The headline average margin over GRPO was revised from 10% (v1) to 6% (v2 camera-ready) while the public artifact still holds v1 numbers; GRPO baseline is a single LoRA run on one 8B model with 8,192 context and 24k rollouts, no hyperparameter sweep, and GRPO was not run on GPT-4.1-mini. (2) Single-seed results, no confidence intervals. (3) System-aware merge hurts on Qwen3-8B (IFBench 38.61 to 28.23; aggregate 61.28 to 57.62), and Pareto selection only clearly beats greedy on Qwen3-8B, not GPT-4.1-mini. (4) Requires a hand-written per-module textual feedback function mu_f; the paper's gains lean on rich feedback, robustness to scalar-only signals is untested. (5) Only instructions evolve, not demos, code, topology or weights (in the paper). (6) Acceptance on a 3-example minibatch is noisy; candidate pool grows unboundedly with full-valset evals per accepted child. (7) Budget counts task-LM metric calls only; reflection-LM (GPT-4.1/GPT-5) cost and the need for a strong reflector are hidden. (8) Reflection prompt encourages memorizing domain facts from training feedback, i.e. distribution-specific prompts; no cross-task or cross-model transfer shown. (9) Round-robin module choice, no credit assignment across modules.
deep_reads.safety_measures: Strict-improvement acceptance on the same minibatch; full validation evaluation of every accepted candidate with per-instance score tracking; Pareto-front selection to avoid collapse; held-out test set for reporting; candidates are immutable tree nodes so the final pick is the best-by-validation (implicit rollback). No content/safety filter on generated prompts, no check for validation leakage into prompts, no adversarial or reward-hacking audit; reflection LM is trusted.
deep_reads.key_insight: Execution traces plus textual evaluator feedback are a far denser learning signal than a scalar reward: an LLM reflecting on a handful of failed trajectories can write rules that generalize, and keeping a per-instance Pareto frontier of candidates (rather than the single best) preserves complementary lessons so the search does not collapse — yielding RL-beating accuracy with ~35x fewer rollouts and no gradient updates.
open_gaps: Only module instructions evolve in the paper; no joint evolution of code, tool set, workflow topology or weights (library's optimize_anything extends this but without the paper's controlled evaluation).
No cross-task or cross-model transfer: learned lessons live inside a task/model-specific prompt and every new task or LM starts from the seed prompt; no reusable memory/skill store across runs.
Fitness is a fixed offline train/val split; no continual or online mode that ingests production traces, detects drift, or re-optimizes incrementally.

Acceptance uses a 3-example minibatch with a strict-improvement rule and no statistical test; noisy accepts are filtered only by a costly full-valset eval, and the candidate pool grows without pruning.
Requires a hand-authored per-module textual feedback function (mu_f); no automatic synthesis of actionable feedback from raw traces or from scalar-only metrics.
Reflection LM and reflection prompt are static and never improved (no meta-level self-improvement, no learning of what kinds of reflections lead to accepted mutations).

No verification/safety layer on proposed prompts: nothing checks for validation-set leakage, memorized answers, or unsafe instructions before acceptance; reflection prompt explicitly encourages baking in domain facts.
Reflection-LM token cost is excluded from the rollout budget; a cost-aware budget (task + reflection tokens) and cheaper reflectors are unaddressed.
Module selection is round-robin; no credit assignment deciding which module caused a failure, and merge is a fixed-count heuristic that regressed on Qwen3-8B.
GRPO comparison is one LoRA run on one 8B model; no study of combining prompt evolution with weight updates (the authors' May 2026 'Fast-Slow' blog only starts this).

deep_reads.name: Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) / Meta Agent Search
deep_reads.org_or_authors: Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, Jeff Clune — University of British Columbia, Vector Institute, Canada CIFAR AI Chair
deep_reads.last_activity: 2025-01-28 (last repo push; arXiv v1 2024-08-15, ICLR 2025 camera-ready early 2025)
deep_reads.venue_or_citations: ICLR 2025 (poster, OpenReview t9U3LW7JVX); Outstanding Paper, NeurIPS 2024 Open-World Agents workshop; Semantic Scholar: 312 citations, 45 influential (2026-09-11)
deep_reads.mechanism: Verified from ShengranHu/ADAS `_mmlu/search.py` + `mmlu_prompt.py`. The unit of evolution is a single Python `forward(self, taskInfo)` function that composes calls to a fixed primitive `LLMAgentBase(output_fields, name, role, temperature)` (base LLM hard-coded to gpt-3.5-turbo-0125). The meta agent (gpt-4o-2024-05-13) is prompted once per generation with: the framework/utility code, a domain description + one example question, the ENTIRE archive dumped as JSON (each entry = thought, name, code, fitness string), a list of "WRONG implementation" anti-patterns, and the instruction to "maximize fitness by proposing interestingly new agents... THINK OUTSIDE THE BOX". It returns {thought, name, code}. Two fixed reflection turns follow in the same chat: Reflexion_1 asks it to judge novelty vs the archive, find implementation bugs, and improve; Reflexion_2 re-applies the anti-pattern checklist. The code is then `exec()`'d in-process and run on a validation slice; if it throws or scores <1% ("All 0 accuracy"), the traceback is appended and the meta agent debugs, up to debug_max=3 times. Any agent that runs is appended to the archive with fitness = "median + 95% bootstrap CI" string — there is no improvement threshold, no parent selection, no pruning, no crossover; the archive is a flat chronological list. The archive is seeded with 7 hand-written baselines (CoT, CoT-SC, Self-Refine, LLM Debate, Step-back, QD, Role Assignment). Runs 25-30 generations, one candidate per generation, single-threaded search. After search, every archived agent is re-scored on a disjoint test slice. The meta agent, reflection prompts, evaluator, and base model never change.
deep_reads.eval_loop: Signal = ground-truth benchmark accuracy (F1 for DROP) of the exec'd forward() on a fixed validation slice: 128 questions (DROP/MGSM/MMLU), 32 questions x5 repeats (GPQA), small ARC subset x5 repeats; reported as median + 95% bootstrap CI string, which is the only feedback the meta agent sees (no per-example traces). No LLM judge. Drift/hacking controls: (1) the meta agent never sees validation questions (only one example) and answers are graded by exact match; (2) held-out test slice (800 questions) scored post hoc for every archived agent; (3) crash / <1% accuracy triggers debug retry rather than archiving. Weaknesses visible in the released `results/*.json`: fitness on 128 examples has a ~±8pp CI and val->test gaps up to 10pp (Self-Refine MMLU val 73.4 -> test 63.5); nothing is ever rejected for being worse than its predecessors, so the archive accumulates regressions (DROP gens 23-26 all scored ~10%); and the paper's headline numbers coincide exactly with the max TEST fitness over the archive, not the max VALIDATION fitness (see limitations).
deep_reads.key_results: All with GPT-3.5-turbo as the base model and GPT-4o as meta agent; numbers read directly from released archives and match the paper. Best-baseline test vs best-discovered test: DROP F1 65.8 -> 79.4 (+13.6); MGSM 39.0 -> 53.4 (+14.4); GPQA 31.6 -> 34.6; MMLU 65.9 -> 69.6; ARC 8.0 -> 13.7 (median over 5 runs). Paper-claimed transfer: MGSM-discovered agent gives +25.9 on GSM8K and +13.2 on GSM-Hard over baselines; agents found with GPT-3.5 keep their edge when swapped to Claude-Haiku, GPT-4, Claude-Sonnet (ARC ~50% on Sonnet per summaries); math agents transferred to DROP/MMLU/GPQA match or beat baselines. ICLR version adds an empty-archive ablation (no baseline seeds) that still beats hand-designed agents. Search trajectories are noisy, not monotone: MGSM's best agent appeared at generation 4 and was never exceeded in 26 further generations.
deep_reads.limitations: (1) Selection bias in headline numbers: the reported best agents are the archive entries with maximal TEST fitness; selecting by validation fitness (the only legitimate signal) gives DROP 70.7 (not 79.4), GPQA 32.3 (not 34.6), MMLU 69.1, ARC 10.7 — gains over baselines shrink to a few points and are within CI on GPQA/MMLU. (2) Fitness is a 128-example single-benchmark score with ±8pp CI; strong val/test disagreement. (3) No acceptance gate or pruning: every runnable candidate is archived, whole archive is dumped into the prompt each generation, so context grows linearly and search is capped at ~30 single-candidate generations. (4) Discovered agents are 10-50x more expensive than CoT (multi-candidate x multi-critic x multi-refinement loops); cost is not an objective. (5) `exec()` of model-written code in-process, no sandbox (README warns). (6) Base model fixed to gpt-3.5-turbo; only OpenAI models supported; repo abandoned since Jan 2025 with 11 open issues. (7) Meta agent, reflection prompts and evaluator are frozen — no meta-level self-improvement (later addressed by DGM / hyperagents). (8) Benchmarks are single-turn QA with exact-match grading; no tool-use, long-horizon or software tasks. "Self-evolving" is accurate for the agent code but the system as a whole is a fixed outer loop.
deep_reads.safety_measures: README warning that untrusted model-generated code is executed; paper discusses risk of self-improving systems and suggests future "safe-ADAS" incorporating Constitutional AI, and argues for transparency. In practice: no sandbox (plain exec with module globals), no network/IO restriction, no timeout, no human approval gate; the only guards are a context-length assertion and a <1%-accuracy rejection.
deep_reads.key_insight: Make the search space Turing-complete code (a forward() over a single FM-call primitive) and let an LLM meta-agent, conditioned on a growing archive of (design, fitness) pairs, write the next candidate — using the archive as stepping stones for in-context "reflection-driven" search rather than as a population under selection.
open_gaps: Select and report by validation fitness with a paired/held-out protocol; the current pipeline's headline numbers are best-of-archive on the test set
Variance-aware acceptance: 128-example fitness with ±8pp CI needs racing/successive-halving or paired bootstrap vs parent before an agent is archived or promoted

No regression gate or pruning: every runnable candidate is archived, so the archive accumulates collapsed agents (DROP gens 23-26 at ~10%) and the full archive is dumped into the prompt, capping search at ~30 generations
Single scalar fitness feedback: the meta agent never sees per-example failures or traces, so it cannot do credit assignment (contrast GEPA/ACE reflective traces)
No cost/latency objective or Pareto front; discovered agents are 10-50x more expensive than CoT (AFlow/EvoFlow later added this)
No sandboxing: exec() of LLM-written code in-process with module globals, network, and no timeout
Meta-level is frozen: the proposer prompt, reflection steps, debug loop and evaluator cannot be modified by the system (DGM/hyperagents gap)
No cross-domain reuse of discovered building blocks as a library; transfer is only tested post hoc by copying the single top agent
One candidate per generation, sequential; no parallel proposal, no crossover between archive entries, no lineage/tree structure
Only single-turn QA benchmarks with exact-match grading; no tool-use, multi-turn, or software-engineering tasks
Hard-coded to OpenAI gpt-3.5/4o via chat.completions JSON mode; repo unmaintained since 2025-01, not packaged for reuse by app developers
